flashcards.back_definition: WPA2 (2004) uses AES-CCMP with a pre-shared key whose four-way handshake can be captured and cracked offline. WPA3 (2018) uses SAE, which resists offline guessing and gives forward secrecy.
flashcards.back_example: A captured WPA2 handshake lets an attacker test millions of passwords at home.
flashcards.back_confusion: Mixed WPA2/WPA3 mode lets an attacker push clients down to WPA2.
flashcards.back_hook: WPA3 makes guessing happen live, one try at a time.

flashcards.front: Which Wi-Fi security options should never be used?
flashcards.back_definition: Open networks for sensitive work, WEP, and WPA with TKIP: all are broken or provide no protection.
flashcards.back_example: A router set to WPA/TKIP mixed mode should be changed to WPA2-AES or WPA3.
flashcards.back_confusion: Hiding the SSID is not a security setting: scanners still see it.
flashcards.back_hook: WEP and TKIP are museum pieces.

flashcards.back_definition: Stealing one key later cannot decrypt sessions recorded in the past, because each session used its own temporary key.
flashcards.back_example: An attacker who learns the Wi-Fi password next year still can't read last year's captured WPA3 traffic.
flashcards.back_confusion: With WPA2-Personal, knowing the password plus the captured handshake can decrypt that session.
flashcards.back_hook: Yesterday stays locked even if today's key leaks.

flashcards.back_definition: Personal uses one shared password for everyone. Enterprise uses 802.1X with a RADIUS server, so each user signs in with their own credentials.
flashcards.back_example: When an employee leaves, Enterprise disables one account; Personal means changing the password for all.
flashcards.back_confusion: Enterprise also gives individual accountability in the logs.
flashcards.back_hook: One key for all vs a key each.

flashcards.front: What did the 2017 KRACK attack break?
flashcards.back_definition: It tricked devices into reinstalling a WPA2 key during the handshake, resetting counters so traffic could be decrypted or replayed. It was fixed by patching devices, not by changing passwords.
flashcards.back_example: Unpatched Android and Linux clients were especially exposed.
flashcards.back_confusion: KRACK attacked the protocol's handshake, not the password strength.
flashcards.back_hook: Key Reinstallation AttaCK: reuse the key, break the lock.

flashcards.front: Name the three families of security controls.
flashcards.back_definition: Managerial (policies, procedures, training), technical (firewalls, encryption, access lists) and physical (locks, badges, fences).
flashcards.back_example: An acceptable use policy is managerial; a firewall rule is technical; a server-room lock is physical.
flashcards.back_confusion: A policy is a real control even though no software enforces it.

flashcards.front: What is an acceptable use policy (AUP)?
flashcards.back_definition: A document that says what users may and may not do with an organisation's systems and data, usually signed when they join.
flashcards.back_example: The AUP bans connecting personal routers to the office network.
flashcards.back_confusion: An AUP sets the rules; technical controls and monitoring enforce them.
flashcards.back_hook: The house rules for the network.

flashcards.back_definition: Access rights pile up over time as people change roles and old permissions are never removed.
flashcards.back_example: A finance employee moved to marketing still has payroll access three years later.
flashcards.back_confusion: Regular access reviews catch it; least privilege says remove what isn't needed now.
flashcards.back_hook: Access only grows unless someone prunes it.

flashcards.front: Does security awareness training actually work?
flashcards.back_definition: When it is regular, practical (with phishing simulations) and measured, it reduces how often staff fall for social engineering.
flashcards.back_example: Click rates on simulated phishing drop after monthly short training.
flashcards.back_confusion: A once-a-year slideshow ticks a box but changes little.

flashcards.front: Name the layers of a layered network defence.
flashcards.back_definition: Human or managerial, perimeter (firewall, IPS, DNS filtering), network (segmentation, Wi-Fi security), host (EDR, host firewall, patching) and data (encryption, DLP).
flashcards.back_example: A phishing link gets past the email filter, but EDR blocks the payload on the laptop.
flashcards.back_confusion: Several medium controls in different layers beat one strong control alone.
flashcards.back_hook: From the gate to the vault.

flashcards.front: What is a single point of failure?
flashcards.back_definition: Any one control or component whose failure alone exposes everything.
flashcards.back_example: A flat network where getting past the perimeter firewall gives access to every server.
flashcards.back_confusion: Defence in depth exists to remove single points of failure.
flashcards.back_hook: If one thing breaks and all is lost, add a layer.

flashcards.front: Why put guests on their own Wi-Fi network?
flashcards.back_definition: A separate guest network, ideally isolated per client, keeps visitors' devices away from internal systems.
flashcards.back_example: Guest SSID with internet-only access; staff SSID on 802.1X.
flashcards.back_confusion: Using the same network with a different password is not isolation.

flashcards.front: What did DEF CON's Wall of Sheep show?
flashcards.back_definition: That people still log in over unencrypted connections on shared Wi-Fi: it publicly displays (partly masked) credentials captured from the conference network.
flashcards.back_example: A username and part of a password from a plain HTTP login appears on the screen.
flashcards.back_confusion: It is an awareness exhibit, not an attack on anyone's account.
flashcards.back_hook: Baa: you sent it in the clear.
